# Probability {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#probability"}

So what is probability? 

::: {.fragment}
It's a way of talking about uncertainty.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- I don't know if it's going to rain tomorrow...
- ...but that doesn't mean I don't know anything.
- In Nepal, rain works differently in June than in January.
:::

::: {.fragment}
But what does _"a 31% chance of rain"_ actually mean? 
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Tomorrow's weather isn't a lottery. Specific physical factors decide it.
- The day isn't random. [But, _**we**_ are uncertain about it.]{.blue} 
- 31% describes our degree of certainty about an uncertain fact.
:::

## Probability is just counting {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#counting"}

_Count everything that could happen. Count the ones you care about. Compare._

::: {.fragment}
- **Probability of rolling a six on a die**:\
  6 sides could land face up. Only one of them is a six.\
  [→ **1 out of 6**]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Probability of winning a raffle**:\
  500 tickets sold. You bought 10.\
  [→ **10 out of 500**]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **The probability that a random person in this class came by bus**:\
  25 of you are here. 15 of you came by bus.\
  [→ **15 out of 25**]{.blue}.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every analysis we do in this course will come down to counting, exactly like this.
:::

## Counting the ways a thing could happen {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#counting-ways"}

_Flip a coin four times. How likely is exactly two heads?_

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r garden-all, opts.label = "garden"}
garden_plot(n = 4)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r garden, opts.label = "garden"}
garden_plot(n = 4, target = 2)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment}
Four events, two possibilities each:

- 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = **16** ways in all
- Exactly two heads: [**6** out of 16]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}

| Heads | 0 | 1 | [2]{.blue} | 3 | 4 |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **Ways** | 1 | 4 | [**6**]{.blue} | 4 | 1 |
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
What we're doing is simple:\
[We list all the ways the world could be, and count them.]{.blue}
:::

## Describing Probability: Convention 1 {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#convention-1"}

_We write a probability as a number between 0 and 1, or as a percentage._

::: {.fragment}
| Number | Percentage | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0% | Impossible |
| 0.02 | 2% | Winning the raffle: 10 ÷ 500 |
| 0.17 | 17% | Rolling a six: 1 ÷ 6 |
| 0.31 | 31% | Rain in Kathmandu: 113 ÷ 365 days |
| 0.5 | 50% | A fair coin landing heads: 1 ÷ 2 |
| 1 | 100% | Certain |
:::

::: {.fragment}
To convert between the two, move the decimal point two places to the right or to the
left.
:::


## Describing Probability: Convention 2 {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#convention-2"}

_We write the probability of an event as P( event )._

::: {.fragment}
| We write | We say | Value |
|---|---|---|
| P( rain tomorrow ) | "the probability of rain tomorrow" | 113 ÷ 365 ≈ 0.31 |
| P( getting heads ) | "the probability of getting heads" | 1 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.5 |
| P( rolling a six ) | "the probability of rolling a six" | 1 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.17 |
| P( winning the raffle ) | "the probability of winning the raffle" | 10 ÷ 500 = 0.02 |
:::

::: {.fragment}
It's just shorthand. Everything inside the brackets is the thing we're unsure about.
:::

## Describing Probability: Convention 3 {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#rain"}

_We make a probability more specific by adding a condition: P( event | condition )._
- P( rain | July ) means [_"the probability of rain, given that it's July."_]{.blue}

::: {.fragment}
|  | Rainy days | Days counted | Probability | % |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| P( rain ) | 565 | 1,825 | **0.31** | (31%) |
| P( rain \| Apr ) | 35 | 150 | **0.23** | (23%) |
| P( rain \| Dec ) | 5 | 155 | **0.03** | (3%) |
| P( rain \| Jul ) | 126 | 155 | **0.81** | (81%) |
| P( rain \| Feb ) | 8 | 140 | **0.06** | (6%) |
:::

::: {.fragment}
Can data from the past five years help predict tomorrow? [Maybe, maybe not.]{.blue .fragment}
:::

## Probability lets us ask questions {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#lets-count"}

_Hands up if you had tea this morning._

{{< include _includes/week1/count-demo.md >}}

::: {.incremental}
- That's not really a probability yet. It's just a fact about this group.
- It becomes a **probability** when we use it to say something we _don't_ know:
  - _"If we pick one student at random, how likely is it they had tea?"_\
  [(Exactly []{.count-k-out} in []{.count-n-out})]{.blue}
  - _"If we poll a random person on the street, how likely is it that they had tea?"_\
  [(Possibly similar, if we're willing to make a few assumptions.)]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every prediction needs assumptions. [Interesting predictions need strong assumptions.]{.blue}
:::


# Probability for Decision Making {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#applied-probability"}

::: {.fragment}
In Nepal, HIV has a prevalence of about 0.1%. We can write that as:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- P( HIV+ ) = 0.001 (0.1%)
:::

::: {.fragment}
With statistical tests and predictions, we talk about two kinds of accuracy:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Sensitivity**: of the people who **have** HIV, the share who test positive.
  - P( test+ | HIV+ ) = **0.99** (true positive)
- **Specificity**: of the people who **don't have** HIV, the share who test negative.
  - P( test– | HIV– ) = **0.97** (true negative)
:::

## Probability for Decision Making (continued) {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#base-rate"}

- Sensitivity P( test+ | HIV+ ): 99%
- Specificity P( test– | HIV– ): 97%

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
But there's something strange here...
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
What about P( HIV+ | test+)? [3.2%]{.fragment fragment-index=2 .red}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}

|[(pop: 100,000)]{.fragment fragment-index=4 .blue}           | Test+                                                            | Test–                                                             |
|----------|------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **HIV+**<br>[(0.1%&nbsp;=&nbsp;100)]{.fragment fragment-index=5 .blue}| P( Test+ \| HIV+ ): **99%**<br>_Sensitivity (True Positive)_<br>[(99)]{.fragment fragment-index=6 .blue}| P( Test– \| HIV+ ): **1%**<br>_Type II Error (False Negative)_<br>[(1)]{.fragment fragment-index=6 .blue}|
| **HIV–**<br>[(99.9%&nbsp;=&nbsp;99,900)]{.fragment fragment-index=5 .blue} | P( Test+ \| HIV– ): **3%**<br>_Type I Error (False Positive)_<br>[(2,997)]{.fragment fragment-index=6 .blue}| P( Test– \| HIV– ): **97%**<br>_Specificity (True Negative)_<br>[(96,903)]{.fragment fragment-index=6 .blue}|
:::

::: {.fragment}

- _Paradox: P(A|B) is not the same as P(B|A)_

[Historical figures for older screening tests. Modern tests reach about 99.8% specificity, which still gives P( HIV+ | test+ ) of only about 33%. In practice, a positive screen is always confirmed with further tests, and the people who get tested have a much higher prevalence than 0.1%.]{.source}
:::


## Direction of conditions

P(A|B) _is not the same as_ P(B|A)

{{< include _includes/week1/cond-table.md >}}


# The base rate paradox {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#base-rate-paradox"}

_When something is rare, most positive results are false, even from an accurate test._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r hiv-all, opts.label = "base_rate"}
base_rate_plot(n_true = 1, true_positives = 1, false_positives = 30)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r hiv-tested, opts.label = "base_rate"}
base_rate_plot(
  n_true = 1,
  true_positives = 1,
  false_positives = 30,
  results = TRUE
)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
1,000 people get tested. Only [1 person has HIV]{.blue}. The test identifies them. 

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
It also flags [30 people who don't have HIV]{.red}.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.big-statement}
31 positives.\
Only 1 is real.
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Statistical significance (revisited) {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#statistical-significance-revisited"}

Let's look at that quote again:

> A result is statistically significant if, [assuming the null hypothesis is true]{.fragment fragment-index=2 .highlight-red} and the model assumptions hold, [the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed]{.fragment fragment-index=3 .highlight-blue} (the p-value) is less than or equal to the chosen significance level α. This leads to rejection of the null hypothesis while controlling the long-run Type I error rate at α.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Two key phrases: 
:::

- ["assuming the null hypothesis is true"]{.fragment .red fragment-index=2}
- ["the probability of...data..."]{.fragment .blue fragment-index=3}

::: {.fragment}
This frames _statistical significance_ as:

- P( [data]{.blue} | [hypothesis]{.red} )
:::

::: {.fragment}
Not the same as (what we usually actually want):

- P( [hypothesis]{.red} | [data]{.blue} )
:::


## The problem with p-values {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#pvalue-direction"}

If statistics has ever made you feel dumb or intimidated, [it's not you]{.blue}. P-value
imagines the world in a very [strange way]{.red}.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

|  | Starts from | Asks |
|---|---|---|
| [**How we observe**]{.fragment fragment-index=2} | [what we [saw]{.blue}]{.fragment fragment-index=2} | [_"What does this tell me about the [world]{.green}?"_]{.fragment fragment-index=2} |
| [**A p-value**]{.fragment fragment-index=3} | [an [imagined world]{.red} with nothing going on]{.fragment fragment-index=3} | [_"How surprising would my [data]{.blue} be there?"_]{.fragment fragment-index=3} |
:::

::: {.incremental}
- A p-value doesn't tell you if a hypothesis is true.
- It tells you how unlikely the data would be if the null hypothesis were true.
- Those aren't the same thing. P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A)
:::

::: {.fragment}
We want a different kind of statistics to work the same way knowledge does: we start with [assumptions]{.red}, we encounter new [data]{.blue}, and we [update our beliefs]{.green} about the world.
:::


# Bayesian Updating

## Bayesian Updating: What it is not
![*Statistical Rethinking*, p.2 (Richard McElreath, 2020)](images/week1/mcelreath-2.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Bayesian Updating: What it is {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#bayesian-updating"}

Instead of a flowchart of tests, [**one rule for all of statistics**]{.blue}:

[**Prior**]{.red} × [**Likelihood**]{.blue} → [**Posterior**]{.green}

::: {.incremental}
- [**Prior**]{.red}: what we believe about the world _before_ seeing the new data
- [**Likelihood**]{.blue}: how likely the data we saw would be, under _each_ possible answer
- [**Posterior**]{.green}: what we believe _after_ combining the two. It challenges the
  prior, or makes it stronger
:::

::: {.fragment .callout-tip title="Example: will the mayor win?"}
::: {.incremental}
- [**Prior**]{.red}: _"He got 60% last time, so I think about 60% of Kathmandu will vote
  for him."_
- [**Likelihood**]{.blue}: _"I took a small survey and only 20% of people said they'll vote for him. That doesn't fit very well with my prior belief of 60% but fits better with lower numbers."_
- [**Posterior**]{.green}: _"I now think about 45% of people will vote for him."_
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
That's it. A poll, a regression, a causal model: everything in this course is just this
[one rule]{.blue}, applied again and again.
:::

## Bayesian Updating Example {.no-title}
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
{{< include shiny/updating.R >}}
```






## Bayes' theorem {.mechanics notes="notes/week1_notes.md#bayes-theorem"}

_The one rule, written as a formula._

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
$$
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) \times P(A)}{P(B)}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
$$
\class{green}{P(\text{belief} \mid \text{data})}
=
\frac{
\class{blue}{P(\text{data} \mid \text{belief})}
\;\times\;
\class{red}{P(\text{belief})}
}{
\class{gray}{P(\text{data})}
}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.incremental}
- [**P( belief )**]{.red}: the **prior**. What we believed before.
- [**P( data | belief )**]{.blue}: the **likelihood**. How likely the data are, if the belief is true.
- [**P( belief | data )**]{.green}: the **posterior**. What we believe now.
- [**P( data )**]{.gray}: Usually not interesting. Just here to rescale total possibilities to 100%.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Conceptually:
[**Prior**]{.red} × [**Likelihood**]{.blue} → [**Posterior**]{.green}
:::


# So why is most published research wrong? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#why-research-wrong"}

_It's the HIV test again._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r ideas-all, opts.label = "base_rate"}
base_rate_plot(n_true = 10, true_positives = 8, false_positives = 50)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r ideas-significant, opts.label = "base_rate"}
base_rate_plot(
  n_true = 10,
  true_positives = 8,
  false_positives = 50,
  results = TRUE
)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
1,000 ideas get tested. Most are wrong: only [10 are true]{.blue}.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Good studies find [8]{.blue} of the true ones.

They also "find" [50]{.red} false ones, by chance.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.big-statement}
58 discoveries.\
Only 8 are real.
:::
:::
:::
:::

## How far can we trust a "discovery"? {.mechanics .smaller notes="notes/week1_notes.md#research-math"}

_α: the chance of a "significant" result when the idea is false · β: the chance of missing an idea that's true_

| Type of study | True ideas | α | β | Chance a "discovery" is true |
|--------------------------------|:--------:|:----:|:----:|:------------:|
| Large trial of a promising idea | 50% | 5% | 20% | **94%** |
| Small study of a promising idea | 50% | 5% | 80% | 80% |
| Search for new effects _(the 1,000 ideas)_ | 1% | 5% | 20% | [14%]{.red} |
| Small search for new effects | 1% | 5% | 80% | [4%]{.red} |
| p-hacked small study | 10% | 20% | 80% | [10%]{.red} |

::: {.fragment}
What matters most is how many of the ideas we test are true to begin with.
:::


# Most studies are wrong. Is that a problem? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#is-that-a-problem"}

_Most studies are wrong._ [...and that's okay.]{.fragment .blue}

::: {.incremental}
- A study was never supposed to be the answer. It's one observation.
- Each observation joins what we already know and nudges it, a little or a lot.
- A single observation never gives us the answer.
- Instead, we use observations to support or challenge what we think we already know.
- Without these prior assumptions, data is meaningless.
:::

## Science is updating {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#science-is-updating"}

What makes science work isn't experiments or observations.

::: {.fragment}
It's [groups of scientists arguing]{.blue} about how to fit many observations together,
observations that often contradict each other.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
Science isn't the experiments we do.\
It's the debates we have about them.
:::
:::

## Objective or subjective? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#objective-subjective"}

> _"Ethnography is subjective. Statistics is objective. It's hard data."_

::: {.fragment}
|                 | Observation                    | Interpretation assumes…                          |
|-----------------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **Ethnography** | interviews, field notes        | what people meant; whose voices stand for others |
| **Statistics**  | surveys, measurements, records | what causes what; how the data were generated    |
:::

::: {.fragment}
Both join an objective part, the observation, with a subjective part, the assumptions.
[The difference isn't the field. It's whether the assumptions are stated openly, where
others can challenge them.]{.blue}
:::

## Doing science {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#doing-science"}

_The math is the least interesting part._

::: {.incremental}
- Nearly every important choice happens before any numbers: what to ask, what to
  observe, who to include, what to assume.
- So we can interpret and critique a statistical argument without the statistical
  mechanics. Ask what it assumes, how the data were made, and what else could explain it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
The science comes first.
:::
:::

## Updating improves our assumptions {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#updating-assumptions"}

::: {.incremental}
- A [**prior**]{.red} is an assumption, written down where others can see it and argue
  with it.
- New [**data**]{.blue} test it: does what we saw fit what we assumed?
- The [**posterior**]{.green} is a better assumption, and the starting point next time.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
Assume, look, update. Repeat.
:::
:::

## Summary {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#summary"}

1. [**Probability is counting**]{.blue}, and direction matters: P( A | B ) ≠ P( B | A ).
2. [**Objective and subjective.**]{.blue} Statistics, like ethnography, joins objective
   observation with subjective assumptions. A study is one observation, not an answer.
3. [**Bayesian updating**]{.blue} is how we improve those assumptions:
   prior × likelihood → posterior.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
The science always comes first.
:::
:::


# What's ahead {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#whats-ahead"}

That's what we're going to do here: [put the science first]{.blue}.

- **Week 2**: distributions. A different way to think about numbers, for populations and for uncertainty.
- **Week 3**: draw our science. Causal diagrams (DAGs) before any model.
- **Week 4**: forks, pipes and colliders. What to control for, and what not to.
- **Week 5**: what did they leave out? Unobserved forks, pipes and colliders.

Every week starts with the question and what we believe about the world.
[The statistics come after.]{.gray}
:::

# Practical work: Will the mayor win? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-demo"}

_Appendix: we'll work through this together with the TA in our second class._

Let's walk through the simplest possible version of this workflow.

- **Estimand**: θ, the share of Kathmandu voters who will vote for the current mayor.
- **Background**: in the last election, the mayor got 60% of the vote.
- **Data**: we survey *n* voters at random, and *k* of them say they will vote for the mayor.

::: {.fragment .callout-note title="A deliberately simple model"}
Each respondent is like a coin flip that comes up "mayor" with probability θ. No weighting,
no turnout, no non-response, no post-stratification. We'll add those later.
:::

## The model, written formally {.mechanics notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-model"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
k &\sim \text{Binomial}(n,\ \theta) && \class{blue}{\text{likelihood}} \\
\theta &\sim \text{your prior} && \class{red}{\text{prior}}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- The first line is the **likelihood**: how the data are generated, given θ.
- The second line is the **prior**: what we believe about θ before any data.
- From Week 3 on, we'll build models like this from a DAG.
:::

## Step 1: The prior {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-prior"}

_Before seeing any survey, what do you believe about θ? Drag the points._

{{< include _includes/week1/poll-prior.md >}}

## Step 2: The likelihood {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-likelihood"}

_We survey 20 voters. 6 of them (30%) say they will vote for the mayor._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r likelihood, opts.label = "half_short", out.width = "100%"}
likelihood_plot(n = 20, k = 6, marks = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
How consistent is "6 of 20" with each possible value of θ?

- If θ = 30%: P( 6 of 20 ) = `r round(dbinom(6, 20, 0.3), 3)`
- If θ = 50%: P( 6 of 20 ) = `r round(dbinom(6, 20, 0.5), 3)`
- If θ = 60%: P( 6 of 20 ) = `r round(dbinom(6, 20, 0.6), 3)`
- If θ = 80%: P( 6 of 20 ) = `r format(signif(dbinom(6, 20, 0.8), 2), scientific = FALSE)`

::: {.fragment}
The likelihood is **not** a belief. It's what the coin-flip process in the world says about
our data, one candidate value of θ at a time.
:::
:::
:::

## Step 3: Prior × likelihood → posterior {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-posterior"}

{{< include _includes/week1/poll-posterior.md >}}

## What to try {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-try"}

- **Flat prior vs. strong prior.** Draw a flat prior, then a narrow one around 60% (last
  election). With the same survey, how far apart are the posteriors?
- **More data.** Keep the survey at 30%, but raise *n* from 20 to 500. What happens to the
  prior's influence?
- **Updating in sequence.** Make the posterior your new prior, then run a second survey.
  Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.
- **Answering the real question.** P( mayor wins ) is a direct statement about the hypothesis
  given the data: [P( hypothesis | data )]{.green}, not a p-value.

::: {.fragment}
*What is the result, and how much does it depend on our assumptions?* This is that question,
in miniature.
:::
